writing_guide: Scenarios are made up for practice. No patient names, dates of birth, addresses or incident numbers.
context: one short line on who the patient is and what happened. Leave it out if the prompt says enough.
prompt: the task, in about 12 words or fewer. Say what to look for: 'Tap the incomplete vitals row', not 'Tap the problem'.
quote: for fix questions, the chart text being fixed. It shows in an 'As charted' box.
explain: two sentences at most. Lead with the rule, then why it matters.
spot charts: one clear problem. Vitals rows use time, hr, bp, rr, spo2 and optional pain; leave a value out to show it was not recorded.
Mix true and false swipe statements, and avoid double negatives.
Options: 3 or 4, each short enough to read in one glance.

sign.name: Sign Last
sign.tip: Sign last — after handoff, once you've read the whole chart.

vitals.name: Abnormal Vitals
vitals.tip: Abnormal is never 'stable.' Recheck it, chart it, report it.

fullset.name: Full Set Every Time
fullset.tip: HR, BP, RR and SpO2 on every set — and recheck after every treatment.

impression.name: Impression Matcher
impression.tip: The impression is why they needed an ambulance, and it must match what you charted.

meds.name: Dose Detective
meds.tip: Drug, dose, units, route, time — for every med, including ones given before you arrived.

psych.name: Psych Pro
psych.tip: Legal status, safety search, SI details, and who consented.

hospice.name: Code Status Keeper
hospice.tip: Code status, the DNR form, and why a car wouldn't do.

narrative.name: No Templates
narrative.tip: Write what you found, in plain objective words — not a checklist.

questions.prompt: It's fine to sign the chart at dispatch and finish it later.
questions.explain: Your signature says the chart is complete and accurate. Sign after transfer of care, once you've reviewed it.

questions.prompt: When should you sign the crew attestation?

options.text: After handoff, once you've reviewed the chart

questions.explain: Sign last. The attestation covers everything in the chart, including the handoff.

questions.prompt: Co-signing your partner's chart means you're vouching for it too.
questions.explain: Your signature covers the whole chart, not just your part. Read it before you sign.

questions.context: You spot a mistake after the chart is locked.
questions.prompt: How do you fix it?

options.text: Add a dated addendum with the correction
Ask someone to delete the chart
Start a new chart for the same call

questions.explain: Fix a locked chart with an addendum that shows when it was added. Never hide or erase the original.

questions.prompt: Before you sign, what's the most important check?

options.text: The narrative agrees with the vitals and meds
The narrative is as short as possible
Your partner's name is spelled right

questions.explain: The chart has to agree with itself. Mismatched vitals, meds and narrative are the first thing a reviewer finds.

questions.prompt: Tap the vitals row that needed a recheck.

narrative.text: Patient walked from bed to cot.
Report given to the receiving nurse.

questions.explain: 170/150 in a teenager is either an emergency or a bad reading — recheck it, manually if needed. Chart both readings and report it.

questions.prompt: A heart rate of 120 the whole ride counts as 'stable' because it never changed.
questions.explain: Stable means normal and unchanged — a steady 120 is persistent tachycardia. Name it, say what you did, and who you told.

questions.prompt: Which rewrite is best?

options.text: BP 118/40, rechecked 120/45. Alert, skin warm and dry. Low diastolic reported to RN.
BP a little low, patient fine.

questions.explain: Name the abnormal value, show the recheck, describe how the patient looked, and say who you told.

questions.prompt: A reading looks wrong. What do you do?

options.text: Replace it with the last reading
Recheck it and chart both readings

questions.explain: Never delete or change a reading. Recheck it and chart what you found, so the chart explains itself.

questions.prompt: Tap the line the vitals don't support.

narrative.text: Patient on 2 L nasal cannula per facility.
Report given to the receiving nurse.

questions.explain: SpO2 fell to 88% while the heart and breathing rates rose — that isn't stable. Chart the change, what you did, and who you told.

questions.context: Patient got IV hydromorphone in the ED before you arrived.
questions.prompt: Tap the incomplete vitals row.

narrative.text: Hydromorphone 1 mg IV given in the ED at 1915.
Patient walked to the cot with one assist.

questions.explain: Every set needs HR, BP, RR and SpO2 — especially after an opioid, when BP and breathing can drop. A blank BP looks like it was never checked.

questions.prompt: What makes a full set of vitals?
questions.explain: HR, BP, RR and SpO2 on every set. Add a pain score when pain is part of the complaint.

questions.prompt: If the patient refuses a BP, leave the BP blank.
questions.explain: Chart it as refused and say so in the narrative. A blank looks like you skipped it.

questions.prompt: When should you take vitals?

options.text: Throughout the ride, and after any change or treatment

questions.explain: Two sets is the floor, not the goal. A long ride needs reassessment along the way.

questions.prompt: After you give a medication, take another set of vitals.
questions.explain: The recheck shows whether the treatment worked or caused harm. Chart the after as well as the before.

questions.context: Hospice patient. SpO2 69% on room air; you place a non-rebreather.
questions.prompt: Best primary impression?
questions.explain: Pick the problem that needed you — here, the low oxygen. A vague impression undersells why the patient needed an ambulance.

questions.context: Colostomy came out at the nursing home; going to the ED to have it replaced.
questions.prompt: Best primary impression?
questions.explain: If they need an ambulance to the ED, 'No apparent illness' contradicts the call. Chart the actual problem.

questions.prompt: Your primary impression should agree with the vitals you charted.
questions.explain: 'Bradycardia' next to a charted heart rate of 75 doesn't hold up. The numbers and the impression should tell the same story.

questions.context: Teen transferred for suicidal thoughts with a plan.
questions.prompt: Best primary impression?
questions.explain: Chart what's actually going on. 'No apparent illness' on an SI transfer undercuts why they needed you.

questions.prompt: When is 'No apparent illness/injury' right on a transfer?

options.text: Almost never — there's a reason they need an ambulance
When you're not sure what to pick

questions.explain: Every ambulance transport has a reason. Chart that reason, even when the patient is stable.

questions.prompt: Which rewrite is best?

options.text: RN gave hydromorphone 0.5 mg IV at 1415, before EMS arrival.

questions.explain: Drug, dose, units, route, time. '.5' could mean mg or mL, and a missing leading zero is a setup for a tenfold error.

questions.prompt: Write a leading zero: 0.5 mg, not .5 mg.
questions.explain: '.5' is easily misread as 5 — a tenfold error. Write 0.5 mg, and never a trailing zero like 5.0 mg.

questions.prompt: Meds the sending facility gave before you arrived don't belong in your chart.
questions.explain: They change what to expect en route — sedation, pain, vitals. Chart drug, dose, units, route and time.

questions.prompt: What's missing from this line?
questions.quote: ATIVAN AND HALDOL GIVEN FOR AGITATION.

options.text: Dose, route and time for each

questions.explain: Sedatives change how you monitor the patient. Every med needs its dose, route and time.

questions.context: Back pain patient leaving the ED.
questions.prompt: Tap the line that's missing doses.

narrative.text: Morphine given twice and Zofran given.
Two-person pivot from bed to cot.

questions.explain: 'Given twice' can't be checked by anyone. Every med needs drug, dose, units, route and time — as the ketorolac line shows.

questions.prompt: Which belongs in every psych transfer narrative?

options.text: Legal status — voluntary or on a hold
How long the ED wait was

questions.explain: Chart legal status, the safety search, SI details, and who consented for a minor. Those protect the patient and you.

questions.context: Patient says they planned to use a knife.
questions.prompt: What must the chart show before you leave?

options.text: That a safety search was done, and what it found

questions.explain: A stated weapon plan makes the safety search essential. Chart that it was done and what turned up.

questions.prompt: 'Calm and cooperative' on its own shows why a psych patient needed an ambulance.
questions.explain: On its own it argues the opposite. Add the reason — for example, active SI with a plan and a need for 1:1 observation.

questions.context: Patient argued about going; the crew said they'd restrain him if he got aggressive.
questions.prompt: Which rewrite is best?
questions.quote: CREW TOLD PT WE WOULD RESTRAIN HIM.

options.text: Pt verbally agitated about transport. Calm de-escalation used; pt agreed to sit on cot. No restraints needed.
Leave it out of the chart.

questions.explain: Chart the behavior, your de-escalation, and the result. Restraint is a protocol decision, not a threat.

questions.context: 12-year-old with suicidal thoughts; mom at bedside.
questions.prompt: What should the chart say about consent?

options.text: Only needed if mom rides along

questions.explain: For a minor, chart who consented and how they're related. That's the legal basis for the transport.

questions.prompt: Every hospice transport chart should state the patient's code status.
questions.explain: If the patient declines en route, code status guides what you do. Note that the DNR form traveled with the patient.

questions.context: Hospice patient going home; the family asks you not to take vitals.
questions.prompt: What do you chart?

options.text: Who declined, their relationship, and what you could see

questions.explain: A refusal is charted, not left blank. Then chart what you can observe — breathing, skin, mental status.

questions.prompt: Which belongs in every hospice transport chart?

options.text: Code status, and that the DNR form traveled with the patient
The family's opinion of the hospital

questions.explain: Code status and the DNR form protect the patient's wishes if something changes en route.

questions.prompt: For a hospice patient going home, you don't need to chart why they needed an ambulance.
questions.explain: Every transport needs a reason a car or wheelchair van wouldn't do — bedbound, on oxygen, unable to sit up. Chart it.

questions.prompt: Which rewrite is best?

options.text: Hospice pt to home. DNR form with pt. Bedbound, on 2 L oxygen, unable to sit upright.

questions.explain: Chart code status and why a car wouldn't do. That protects the patient's wishes and shows the transport was needed.

questions.prompt: 'On scene, primary, secondary, vitals, pt to cot' is a complete narrative.
questions.explain: That's a checklist, not a narrative. It says you assessed — not what you found.

questions.context: Ventilator patient going to a long-term acute care hospital.
questions.prompt: Tap the line that needs more detail.

narrative.text: Patient on ventilator, opens eyes to voice.
Care transferred to the receiving nurse with report.

questions.explain: 'Per sending hospital' tells the next crew nothing. Chart the mode, rate, tidal volume, FiO2 and PEEP.

questions.prompt: Your narrative says 'without incident' seven times. The fix?

options.text: Say it once; use the space for what you found
Delete the narrative and rely on the fields

questions.explain: Swapping the phrase isn't a fix. The next caregiver needs what you observed.

questions.context: This line was meant to describe the patient.
questions.prompt: Which rewrite is best?
questions.quote: CREW STATED THEY DID NOT FEEL PAIN.
questions.explain: As written, it says the crew had no pain. Reread before you submit — who did what matters in a legal record.

questions.prompt: When the patient describes a symptom, quoting their own words is good practice.
questions.explain: A direct quote like "my chest feels tight" is objective and hard to dispute. It beats your summary of what they meant.

questions.prompt: Which is the most objective?

options.text: Odor of alcohol, slurred speech, unsteady when standing.

questions.explain: Chart what you saw, heard and smelled. Labels like 'drunk' can be wrong and invite challenge.
